question: Torrential rains caused by the DANA weather phenomenon have affected a large area of southern and eastern Spain, where the worst floods in a century have been recorded. This natural catastrophe has left a horrifying scene in its wake: more than 200 deaths, numerous missing persons, millions of euros of damage and thousands of people left homeless.

A week later, the affected areas are still covered in sludge, stagnant water and sewerage, and are thus breeding grounds for numerous diseases, infections and, in extreme cases, epidemics. At this moment in time, the authorities are concerned about the possibility of a tetanus epidemic among affected persons and volunteers who may have had open wounds and come into contact with contaminated sludge.
There has therefore been a push in the affected areas for people to get vaccinated against this disease. 1.
Is the Commission in a position to contribute to mitigating the risk of vaccine shortages in the event of natural disasters such as the one in Spain?
Has the Spanish Government requested the EU rescue mechanism (rescEU) to be activated in order to obtain medical aid and assistance with disease prevention?
Has a virtual warehouse for data on vaccine needs and stocks already been set up to provide information on vaccine supplies and shortages?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.1.2025) The European Medicines Agency (EMA), together with the Member States, continuously monitors and investigates signals of potential supply disruptions escalated to EU level by national competent authorities to prevent their occurrence and mitigate their effects as far as possible.

The potential impact of the situation in Spain on the supply of medicinal products is closely monitored. Thus far, no critical shortage requiring EU coordination actions has been identified in this context.

In the context of the flood emergency and upon request from the Spanish authorities, the EU Copernicus satellite mapping system1 was activated on 29 October 2024, and the EU Civil Protection Mechanism2, on 8 November 2024. As a result, 83 maps were produced, and several Member States offered in-kind assistance, in the form of heavy vehicles and pumps.

The Commission deployed two liaison officers to help coordinate the assistance. The EU’s strategic reserve, rescEU,3 was not mobilised as the requests were fulfilled by the offers of Member States. A virtual warehouse for data on vaccine needs and stocks has not been set up yet, apart from the existing IT tool CECIS 2.0, in the area of civil protection.

As part of the implementation of EMA’s extended mandate4, the European Shortages Monitoring Platform, launched in November 2024, will be used to report shortages and monitor supply, demand, and stock levels of medicinal products for preparedness activities, and during a public health emergency or major event.
As part of the pharmaceutical reform5, the Commission has proposed to further expand the platform to cover structural shortages and security of supply of critical medicines.
